name: California
verdict: Its 340B hospitals cleared {netIncomeWords} in a year and take an estimated {exemptionsWords} in tax breaks. No state permit stands between a physician and a new facility. The attorney general must consent to every nonprofit hospital sale and writes charity care into the terms. Just over half of their {contractPharmacies} contract pharmacy arrangements are with pharmacies outside California.
gradeNote: Driver grades I and III follow the Build Brief 2 scale (November 6, 2026). Grades IV and V are provisional Alliance grades, open until the state-grade rubric is published at /methodology/state-grade/.

stateIncomeTax.note: California corporation franchise tax at 8.84% on the same base.

propertyTax.note: Hospitals in Los Angeles County at the Los Angeles rate, all others at the Yreka rate, on land, land improvements and buildings at historical cost. Three hospitals whose cost reports leave the county blank (two in Los Angeles, one in West Hills) are counted in Los Angeles County.

systems.subtitle: Their 340B hospitals in California
systems.note: Margin is net income over net patient revenue plus other income, the cost report's total margin. CMS hospital cost reports, latest report per hospital; hospitals assigned to systems by the AHRQ 2023 Compendium linkage. 50 of the {inCostReport} are public hospitals (hospital districts, counties and the University of California) and file no Form 990. Every one of the {hospitals} hospitals has a cost report.

drivers.label: Section 6001
drivers.title: Physician-owned hospitals
drivers.body: The federal ban applies here as everywhere. California has {pohOperating} physician-owned hospitals still operating under the grandfather clause, of {pohListed} on the Alliance list. They are Hoag Orthopedic Institute in Irvine and Patients' Hospital of Redding. One more runs as a joint venture with a health system; two closed and three were sold. No new one can open and bill Medicare.
drivers.source: Alliance physician-owned hospital database (research/poh/poh_db_2026-03.json, March 2026): California {pohListed} hospitals listed; status Operating {pohOperating} (Hoag Orthopedic Institute, Irvine; Patients' Hospital of Redding), Joint Venture 1 (Fresno Surgical Hospital), Closed 2, Sold/Acquired 3

drivers.label: Price Transparency
drivers.title: A chargemaster on request
drivers.body: California's price law dates to 2003. Health and Safety Code 1339.51 makes a hospital post or hand over its charge description master, the gross charge list. Section 1339.585 gives an uninsured patient a written estimate on request. The state sets no machine-readable file and no shoppable-services list of its own. The federal rule does that work. Graded when the rubric is published.
drivers.status: STATE LAW IN FORCE · Rubric pending
drivers.source: California Health and Safety Code section 1339.51 (Payers' Bill of Rights, added by Stats. 2003, Ch. 582, effective January 1, 2004; charge description master available from July 1, 2004; small and rural hospitals exempt) and section 1339.585 (written estimate for a person without health coverage, as amended by Stats. 2021, Ch. 465, AB 532, effective January 1, 2022), leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, retrieved November 21, 2026

drivers.label: Certificate of Need
drivers.title: No permit to compete
drivers.body: California's certificate of need program ended on January 1, 1987, and the statute was repealed in 1995. A hospital needs a license under Health and Safety Code 1250 and nothing more. A physician can build a surgery center or hospital without a competitor's say. Since 2024 the Office of Health Care Affordability reviews large deals for cost and market impact. It reports; it cannot block.
drivers.linkText: Read the certificate of need desk
drivers.source: Stats. 1984, Ch. 1745 (former Health and Safety Code section 439.7: certificate of need requirements inoperative from January 1, 1987); Stats. 1995, Ch. 415 (repeal of the former Division 1 planning statutes); California Health and Safety Code section 1250 (licensing of health facilities); Health and Safety Code section 127507 (Office of Health Care Affordability cost and market impact review, added by Stats. 2022, Ch. 47, as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 641, effective January 1, 2026; the office analyzes and reports); the CON desk's rankings (data/rankings.json: California, no CON law, Free Market tier, score 0)

drivers.label: Hospital Subsidies
drivers.title: {exemptionsWords} a year in tax breaks
drivers.body: Estimated federal, state and property tax exemptions for the {inCostReport} hospitals in the 340B program come to {exemptionsWords} a year. Against that, {charityWords} of charity care at cost. California ties no charity care standard to the exemption. Health and Safety Code 127405 makes every hospital offer charity care or discounts to patients at or below 400 percent of the poverty level. Those hospitals run {childSites} 340B child sites and {contractPharmacies} contract pharmacy arrangements.
drivers.status: NO STANDARD · Discount law at 400% FPL
drivers.source: Estimate from CMS hospital cost reports (2023 and 2024 files, latest report per hospital): federal income tax {federalTaxExact} (21% of net income of the {positiveNetIncome} profitable hospitals, {positiveNetIncomeSumExact}); state franchise tax {stateTaxExact} (8.84% on the same base, Revenue and Taxation Code section 23151); property tax {propertyTaxExact} on {propertyAtCostExact} of land, land improvements and buildings at historical cost, at the Lincoln Institute / Minnesota Center for Fiscal Excellence 50-State Property Tax Comparison Study effective commercial rates for taxes paid in 2025 (Los Angeles 1.187% for Los Angeles County hospitals, Yreka 1.061% elsewhere); total {exemptionsExact}; charity care at cost {charityExact}; California Health and Safety Code section 127405(a) (charity care and discount payment policies for patients at or below 400 percent of the federal poverty level, as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 511, AB 2297) and sections 127340 to 127360 (community benefit plans, no bearing on tax status); HRSA 340B OPAIS export of September 29, 2026 ({childSites} child sites, {contractPharmacies} arrangements)
drivers.as_of: exemptions at 2025 rates on hospital fiscal years ending {fiscalYears}

drivers.label: CMS Favoritism
drivers.title: Urban hospitals, rural rules
drivers.body: {dual} of the {inCostReport} are hospitals in urban areas that CMS treats as rural under 42 CFR 412.103. Cedars-Sinai, Stanford Health Care, Ronald Reagan UCLA and UCSF Medical Center are among them. Rural status can lower the 340B eligibility bar for a rural referral center and change Medicare wage-index reclassification. {projectedDsh} of the {inCostReport} are projected to draw Medicare DSH payments in fiscal 2027, with {ucpWords} in uncompensated care payments.
drivers.source: CMS hospital cost reports (Rural Versus Urban = rural) against the CMS FY2027 IPPS final rule impact file, correction notice (urban geographic classification with the Section 401 flag): {dualNames}; CMS FY2027 IPPS Medicare DSH supplemental file: {projectedDsh} California 340B hospitals projected to receive DSH in FY2027, total uncompensated care payment {ucpExact}
drivers.as_of: CMS FY2027 IPPS final rule impact file (correction notice) and DSH supplemental file

drivers.label: Stark & Anti-Kickback
drivers.title: No room to build rivals
drivers.body: California has its own anti-kickback and self-referral laws. Business and Professions Code 650 makes it a crime to pay or accept anything of value for patient referrals. A first conviction carries up to a year in jail, a $50,000 fine, or both. Section 650.01, the Physician Ownership and Referral Act, covers imaging, laboratory and six other services. A physician cannot refer to an entity in which the physician holds a financial interest. Welfare and Institutions Code 14107.2 adds a Medi-Cal kickback crime. Whether these go beyond the federal statutes is not yet researched.
drivers.source: California Business and Professions Code section 650 (unearned rebates for referrals; first conviction up to one year in county jail or a fine up to $50,000, or both, as amended by Stats. 2021, Ch. 439) and section 650.01 (referrals for laboratory, diagnostic nuclear medicine, radiation oncology, physical therapy, physical rehabilitation, psychometric testing, home infusion therapy and diagnostic imaging barred where the licensee or immediate family has a financial interest, as amended by Stats. 2020, Ch. 265); Welfare and Institutions Code section 14107.2 (Medi-Cal kickbacks); leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, retrieved November 21, 2026; state self-referral review not yet done

agOversight.subtitle: What the office can do, and what it has done

items.title: Consent to every hospital deal
items.body: Corporations Code 5914 and 5920 cover every nonprofit hospital. Before it sells or hands control of a material amount of its assets, it needs the attorney general's written consent. That holds whether the buyer is for-profit or nonprofit. The office has 90 days to decide, with a 45-day extension. Its regulations let it attach conditions.
items.source: California Corporations Code sections 5914 and 5920 (as amended by Stats. 2017, Ch. 782, AB 651), 5915 and 5921 (90-day decision period, 45-day extension), 5925 (regulations); California Code of Regulations title 11, section 999.5; leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, retrieved November 21, 2026

items.title: Charity care written into the deals
items.body: Consent comes with conditions, and charity care levels are among them. The office consented to the Dignity Health and Catholic Health Initiatives combination on November 21, 2018 on conditions. It consented to Cedars-Sinai's affiliation with Huntington Hospital on December 10, 2020 on conditions. On July 2, 2024 it settled with the University of California over its Dignity Health hospital purchase with an assurance of voluntary compliance.
items.source: Office of the Attorney General, nonprofit health facility transaction decisions: Dignity Health / Catholic Health Initiatives (conditional consent, November 21, 2018); Cedars-Sinai Health System / Huntington Memorial Hospital (conditional consent, December 10, 2020); People ex rel. Bonta v. Regents of the University of California, San Francisco Superior Court No. CGC-24-615801, assurance of voluntary compliance filed July 2, 2024 (UCSF Health acquisition of Saint Francis Memorial Hospital and St. Mary's Medical Center from Dignity Health); oag.ca.gov, saved October 1, 2026

items.title: Charity care letters
items.body: On June 14, 2022 the attorney general issued a consumer alert on hospital charity care. The office also wrote to hospitals about their duties under the Hospital Fair Pricing Act. No enforcement suit on charity care has been found.
items.source: Office of the Attorney General press release and consumer alert of June 14, 2022 (hospital charity care obligations under Health and Safety Code sections 127400 to 127446); oag.ca.gov search for charity care enforcement actions, October 1 and November 21, 2026: no suit found

items.title: The 340B program: billing, not spending
items.body: The office polices how hospitals bill Medi-Cal for 340B drugs, not what they keep. On November 2, 2020 it announced an $18.9 million settlement with Memorial Health Services for billing Medi-Cal above acquisition cost on 340B drugs. On February 5, 2024 it announced a $2.1 million settlement with Pomona Valley Hospital Medical Center on the same theory. On December 14, 2020 it led a multistate letter pressing HHS to make drug makers keep supplying 340B discounts to contract pharmacies.
items.source: Office of the Attorney General press releases: Attorney General Becerra Announces $18.9 Million California Settlement with Memorial Health Services (November 2, 2020); Attorney General Bonta Announces $2.1 Million Settlement Against Pomona Hospital for Medi-Cal Fraud (February 5, 2024); Attorney General Becerra Leads Bipartisan Coalition on 340B Drug Pricing Program Requirements (December 14, 2020); oag.ca.gov, saved November 21, 2026 (research/states/sources/ca/)

items.title: Market review beside the office
items.body: Since January 1, 2024 the Office of Health Care Affordability takes 90 days' notice of material deals. It can run a cost and market impact review. Deals already under attorney general review are exempt from the notice but can be referred for a review.
items.source: California Health and Safety Code section 127507 (Stats. 2022, Ch. 47, as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 641, AB 1415, effective January 1, 2026): subdivisions (c)(3) (90-day notice), (d)(4) (exemption for transactions under Corporations Code article 2 review) and (e) (referral for cost and market impact review); leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, retrieved November 21, 2026

rows.title: 340B contract pharmacy protection, clinics only
rows.body: Would bar manufacturers from limiting 340B drug shipments to contract pharmacies used by clinics and health centers. Hospitals are not covered. Passed the Assembly 44 to 6 on May 19, 2025. Senate Health postponed its hearing on July 16, 2025 and never took it up.

rows.title: No PBM discrimination against 340B entities
rows.body: Bars pharmacy benefit managers from paying 340B covered entities and their pharmacies less, excluding them from networks or clawing back the discount. In force since January 1, 2024.

rows.title: Charity care without an application
rows.body: From July 1, 2027, hospitals must screen patients for charity care and discount eligibility before billing them, using data they already hold.

rows.title: Charity care, no asset test
rows.body: Bars hospitals from counting a patient's assets in charity care decisions, from setting application deadlines, and from placing liens on homes to collect. In force since January 1, 2025.

rows.title: Medical debt off credit reports
rows.body: Bars medical debt from California credit reports. A debt a hospital knowingly reports becomes void and unenforceable. In force since January 1, 2025.
